title.en: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
The pillar that does not rust

text.en: In Mehrauli, Delhi, stands an iron pillar about 1,600 years old. Left out in the rain, a bicycle would rust in a year, yet this pillar has stood in the open for centuries almost without rusting. It was probably first erected in front of the Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh and brought to Delhi a few centuries later. It is a symbol of Gupta-era skill. In this chapter we meet the Guptas and the creative age they led.

After the Kushanas and Satavahanas new kingdoms arose, and the new actor on the stage was the Gupta dynasty, which gave the period lasting importance. Samudragupta, a devotee of Vishnu whose mount Garuda appears on inscriptions, defeated many kings. Some were reinstated and paid tribute, while others submitted out of fear of his might. He is shown in coins playing the veena, and a special coin commemorated a great sacrifice. Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramaditya, expanded the empire further and his court is remembered for its scholars and artists.
Rather than controlling everything from a central authority, the Guptas divided the empire into provinces and granted land to local rulers, priests and chieftains. Local kings, including the Pallavas, kept their thrones as long as they accepted Gupta rule and paid tribute. Revenue came from land taxes and also from fines, taxes on mines, irrigation, trade and crafts. Stability strengthened the economy and let the state support scholars, artists and scientists. Alliances, including matrimonial alliances, were one method of building friendship. Kautilya had advised rulers to form alliances (mitra) as one of the seven parts (saptanga) of a state.
The Pallavas of Kanchipuram rose after the Satavahanas and ruled till the 9th century CE. They were great patrons of art and architecture. In the northeast the Kamarupa kingdom of the Varman dynasty extended over the Brahmaputra valley, broadly present-day Assam, and parts of north Bengal and Bangladesh.
The Chinese traveller Faxian (Fa-Xian) visited India in the early 5th century CE and described the society, its cities, its prosperity and its care for the poor and sick. His account is one valuable source, but we must compare many sources and perspectives before drawing conclusions. The Indian Ocean trade network linked Indian ports to distant markets, bringing wealth and ideas.
Aryabhata gave formulas for the motions of the Sun, the Moon and planets, and proposed that the Earth spins on its axis, which explains day and night. In mathematics he described calculation and equation-solving techniques that we still learn at school, first formulated about 1,500 years ago. He observed the world, applied logic and combined it with tradition, making him a pioneer of science. The Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita, which laid the foundation of Ayurveda, were compiled and given final shape in this period. Knowledge from earlier eras was gathered into many texts.
Sanskrit literature flourished. Kalidasa's Meghaduta tells of a yaksha, a minor deity banished by his master, who sends a message to his beloved through a passing cloud. Sarnath near Varanasi is known for exquisite sculptures of the Buddha, and the awe-inspiring Ajanta caves in Maharashtra have famous paintings. Gupta-era temples such as the one near Sanchi and the Udayagiri caves are in Madhya Pradesh. The influence of this age on art, science, literature and governance stretched far beyond the empire and for centuries.

problem.en: Why is the Iron Pillar of Delhi remarkable?

text.en: It is about 1,600 years old and made of iron.
Iron normally rusts quickly in rain, but the pillar has hardly rusted.
It shows the great metallurgical skill of the Gupta age.

prompt.en: Describe three areas in which the Gupta age was creative.

requiredIdeas.en: Art and literature: Ajanta, Sarnath, Kalidasa.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the Gupta empire had one central ruler controlling everything.
Mixing up the Guptas and Mauryas.

points.en: The Guptas ruled from about the 4th century CE, with Samudragupta and Chandragupta II as great rulers.
They governed through provinces and local rulers who paid tribute.
Aryabhata, Charaka and Sushruta, Kalidasa and Ajanta show a creative age.
Faxian's account is a valuable source.
